body:
Meaning of intellectual property

Intellectual property (IP) refers to creations of the human mind, including literary and artistic works, inventions, distinctive business signs and industrial designs. Intellectual-property rights (IPRs) provide legally recognised control over specified uses of these creations or signs.

Unlike a physical object, intellectual property is intangible. A person may own a printed book, but ownership of that copy does not automatically give the person the copyright needed to publish additional copies. Similarly, buying a product carrying a famous brand does not transfer ownership of the brand's trademark.

IP laws seek to encourage creativity, innovation and fair competition while recognising limitations that protect public access, education and other legitimate interests. The rights granted are not unlimited: their subject matter, duration, territorial application and exceptions depend on the relevant law.

The 3 forms of protection

Copyright, trademarks and industrial designs protect different aspects of intellectual activity. Their central distinction is the subject matter being protected.

IP rightProtectsPrincipal Indian lawTypical example
CopyrightOriginal expression in eligible creative worksCopyright Act, 1957Textbook, photograph, computer program
TrademarkA distinctive sign identifying commercial originTrade Marks Act, 1999Brand name or logo
Industrial designEligible visual appearance of an articleDesigns Act, 2000Novel ornamental lamp housing

One product can involve several IP rights

Consider a manufacturer selling a decorative desk lamp. The original wording and illustrations in its instruction manual may receive copyright protection. Its distinctive brand name and logo may function as trademarks. The lamp's new ornamental exterior may qualify for registration as an industrial design.

The electrical operating principle of the lamp is not protected merely because its exterior is registered as an industrial design. Likewise, a competitor's use of a confusing brand name raises a trademark issue rather than automatically becoming a copyright dispute.

Creation and registration are not the same

Copyright generally arises automatically when an eligible original work is created. A formal registration is not a condition for acquiring copyright.

Trademark rights may develop through commercial use, and unregistered marks may receive protection against passing off. Registration, however, provides the statutory right to bring a trademark-infringement action.

Protection under the Designs Act depends on registration. An attractive product does not receive a registered-design monopoly merely because someone created it.

Remember the central distinction: Copyright protects creative expression; trademarks distinguish commercial origin; industrial designs protect qualifying visual features of articles.

Why these rights matter to consumers and industries

Copyright allows creators and authorised owners to control specified uses of protected works. Trademarks help consumers distinguish businesses and reduce confusion about the source of goods and services. Industrial-design protection helps businesses protect original product appearances against unauthorised commercial imitation.

These rights also have economic value. Subject to legal requirements, owners can authorise others to use protected material through licensing arrangements. A manufacturer may license a brand, a publisher may license a translation, and a registered-design proprietor may authorise another manufacturer to apply the protected design.

Prelims focus

  • Copyright is primarily governed by the Copyright Act, 1957.
  • Trademarks are principally governed by the Trade Marks Act, 1999.
  • Industrial designs are governed by the Designs Act, 2000.
  • Copyright protection generally arises without compulsory registration.
  • Trademark infringement and registered-design piracy depend on statutory registration rights.
  • Trap: Owning a physical copy of a creative work does not necessarily mean owning its copyright.

[Sources: Intellectual Property India, Basics of Copyright, Basics of Trademarks and Basics of Designs, consulted 14 November 2026; Copyright Act, 1957, Sections 13–15; Trade Marks Act, 1999, Sections 27–29; Designs Act, 2000, Sections 2, 5 and 11; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 1, Crafts Heritage.]

title: Intellectual Property: Understanding Copyright, Trademarks and Industrial Designs

body:
What copyright protects

Copyright is a legal right that gives the copyright owner exclusive control over certain uses of protected works, subject to statutory limitations and exceptions.

Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957 identifies the principal classes of protected works. Originality is expressly required for literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. Cinematograph films and sound recordings are also protected, subject to the Act's conditions.

Class of workExamplesImportant distinction
LiteraryBooks, articles, poems, computer programsProtects original expression, not merely literary quality
DramaticPlays and eligible choreographic worksConcerns dramatic expression rather than the idea of a performance
MusicalOriginal musical compositionsMusic can be protected separately from song lyrics
ArtisticPaintings, drawings, photographs, sculpturesArtistic merit is not always required
Cinematograph filmFilms and eligible video recordingsFilm protection can coexist with rights in underlying works
Sound recordingRecorded songs, speeches and other soundsProtects the recording separately from underlying compositions

Originality does not mean absolute novelty

For copyright purposes, originality principally concerns independent creation involving the legally required degree of skill, judgment or creativity. A work need not introduce a completely new subject.

For example, 2 authors may independently write textbooks explaining photosynthesis. The scientific subject and established facts are available to both. However, each author's independently created explanations, illustrations and arrangement may receive protection where they meet the originality requirement.

Copyright does not prevent another person from learning the subject, using the underlying facts or writing an independent explanation.

Ideas and expressions are different

Idea–expression distinction: Copyright protects the original manner in which an idea is expressed, not the underlying idea, principle, method or fact itself.

Suppose a writer creates a story about a student who discovers an ancient manuscript. The broad idea of such a discovery is not exclusively owned by that writer. Another writer may develop an independently written story around the same general idea.

However, substantially reproducing protected dialogue, passages or other original expressive elements may infringe copyright even when the reproducer changes the title or uses a different medium.

Facts, information and compilations

Historical dates, scientific discoveries and other facts are not protected merely because they appear in a copyrighted book. Nevertheless, an original selection or arrangement of material may receive copyright protection if it meets the applicable originality standard.

Similarly, a database can qualify as a literary work, but this does not mean that the database owner automatically owns every individual fact recorded in it.

Computer programs are literary works

Section 2(o) expressly includes computer programs, tables and compilations, including computer databases, within literary works.

Therefore, eligible original software code can receive copyright protection. The general idea behind an application, however, is different from the original code or other protected expression used to implement it.

Two programmers may independently create programs performing similar functions. Similar functionality alone does not establish copying of protected expression.

Several copyrights can exist in one audiovisual production

A recorded educational video may contain a separately protected script, musical composition, sound recording, artistic illustrations and cinematograph film.

The owner of the completed film does not necessarily own every underlying work incorporated into it. The relevant authorship, employment, assignment and licensing arrangements must be considered.

Copyright registration

Copyright normally exists as soon as an eligible work is created. Registration with the Copyright Office is optional rather than a prerequisite for protection.

Registration can assist in proving ownership because entries in the Register of Copyrights have evidentiary value. However, a registration certificate does not turn an unprotectable idea into copyrightable subject matter.

A copyright notice, online publication or commercial sale is not what creates copyright. An eligible original work can receive protection even if it remains unpublished.

Copyright and printed learning material

The development of printing made written material easier to reproduce and distribute. Modern digital technologies have extended that ability to electronic books, recordings, software and online learning resources.

Both printed and digital copies may reproduce protected expression. The medium may change, but the copyright question still concerns the protected work, the relevant exclusive right and any applicable exception or permission.

Prelims focus

  • Section 13 specifies the principal classes of works in which copyright subsists.
  • Section 2(o) includes computer programs and computer databases within literary works.
  • Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works receive protection subject to the Act.
  • Copyright protects expression rather than an underlying idea or fact.
  • Copyright registration is not compulsory for acquiring protection.
  • Trap: A film, its screenplay and its music may involve different copyrights.

[Sources: Copyright Act, 1957, Sections 2 and 13–14, Copyright Office; Intellectual Property India, Basics of Copyright, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World – II, Class 10, Chapter 7, Print Culture and the Modern World.]

title: Copyright: Protected Works and the Idea–Expression Distinction

body:
Authorship and ownership are not identical

The author is the person identified as the creator of a particular category of work under the Copyright Act. The copyright owner is the person or entity legally entitled to exercise the economic rights in that work.

The same person may be both author and owner, but this is not always the case.

Section 2(d) identifies the author differently according to the type of work:

  • Literary or dramatic work: the author of the work.
  • Musical work: the composer.
  • Artistic work other than a photograph: the artist.
  • Photograph: the person taking the photograph.
  • Cinematograph film or sound recording: the producer, meaning the person taking the initiative and responsibility for making it.
  • Computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work: the person who causes the work to be created, as stated in the Act.

Who becomes the first copyright owner?

Section 17 establishes the general rule that the author is the first owner of copyright, subject to specified exceptions.

Independent creators

A writer independently creating a book ordinarily becomes its first copyright owner. Similarly, an artist independently creating a painting ordinarily owns its copyright unless a legal exception or relevant agreement changes the position.

Employment

Where a qualifying work is created in the course of employment under a contract of service, the employer is generally the first owner unless an agreement provides otherwise, subject to the specific statutory provisions.

This does not mean that every person who pays for creative work automatically owns the copyright. A freelance contractor and a regular employee may have different legal positions.

Commissioned photographs and specified works

Section 17 contains a specific rule for a photograph taken, a painting or portrait drawn, an engraving made, or a cinematograph film made for valuable consideration at another person's instance. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, the commissioning person is generally the first owner under that provision.

The provision does not establish an unrestricted rule transferring copyright in every commissioned literary or artistic work.

Government works

For a Government work, the Government is ordinarily the first owner unless there is an agreement to the contrary. The Act also contains special provisions for certain public undertakings and other categories.

Exclusive economic rights under Section 14

Section 14 defines copyright through specified exclusive acts. Depending on the category of work, the owner may control:

  • Reproduction: making copies of protected expression, including electronic reproduction.
  • Issue of copies: distributing copies to the public in circumstances covered by the Act.
  • Public performance or communication: performing or communicating the work to the public.
  • Translation: preparing a translation of a protected literary, dramatic or musical work.
  • Adaptation: transforming a protected work into another relevant form.
  • Specified recording and film rights: making films or sound recordings where the Act reserves those acts to the owner.

These rights vary by category of work. Copyright is not one identical bundle of permissions for every type of creative material.

Assignment and licensing

Assignment transfers ownership of specified copyright rights from the assignor to the assignee. Under Section 19, an assignment must be in writing and signed by the assignor or an authorised agent. It must identify the work and specify the rights assigned, duration and territorial extent.

Licensing permits another person to exercise specified rights while ownership need not be transferred. Section 30 provides for licences by copyright owners in writing.

For example, an author may license a publisher to print an English edition without transferring every right in the work. Permission to print the English edition does not necessarily include permission to produce a Gujarati translation or sell electronic editions; the agreement and the applicable law determine the scope.

Moral rights under Section 57

Copyright law recognises certain moral rights of authors independently of economic ownership.

These include the right to claim authorship and the right to restrain or seek damages for certain distortions, mutilations, modifications or other acts relating to a work when they prejudice the author's honour or reputation.

Such rights may continue even after assignment of economic copyright. They are subject to the conditions and qualifications in Section 57.

Economic rights concern specified commercial and other uses of the work. Moral rights principally protect the author's connection with the work and reputation under Section 57.

Prelims focus

  • Section 2(d) identifies authors according to the category of work.
  • Section 14 defines the exclusive acts comprising copyright.
  • Section 17 generally makes the author the first owner, subject to exceptions.
  • Sections 18–19 address assignment of copyright.
  • Section 57 protects specified special rights of authors.
  • Trap: A person who commissions creative work does not automatically own every category of copyright merely by paying for it.

[Sources: Copyright Act, 1957, Sections 2(d), 14 and 17–19, Chapter IV, Ownership of Copyright and Rights of the Owner; Sections 30 and 57, Copyright Office, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Section 17 links first ownership to the legal relationship; assignment transfers economic rights, while moral rights exist independently.
pictures.caption: The first owner depends on the type of work and the legal relationship under which it was created.

title: Copyright: Authorship, Ownership, Economic Rights and Moral Rights
